content: The World Health Organization (WHO) provides specific guidance on defining HIV cases and integrating these definitions into existing patient monitoring systems. This ensures a standardized approach to tracking and managing HIV infections. Key population (KP) data is critical for understanding access to healthcare services among vulnerable groups. However, confidentiality and data security are of utmost importance when collecting KP-related information, whether through patient monitoring or case surveillance systems. In most cases, patient records should not explicitly include KP categories. Instead, any collected data should primarily support patient management and referrals to care. The probable route of HIV transmission can be assessed at the time of diagnosis and used to disaggregate data in HIV case surveillance systems. WHO offers guidance on addressing challenges related to KP data collection and reporting. Countries are encouraged to transition progressively from paper-based to electronic patient information systems, particularly in settings with more than 2,000 patients. WHO provides a tiered approach as an example for this transition. Additionally, countries should establish and strengthen various levels of data security, investing in robust databases and policies to protect confidentiality based on specific risks and benefits. WHO outlines major headings and references additional specialized guidance for this purpose. HIV case surveillance involves reporting the initial diagnosis of HIV infection and defined sentinel events to public health agencies responsible for monitoring and controlling the epidemic. Sentinel events include HIV diagnosis, entry into care, first CD4 count, initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART), viral suppression, and death. Information from each case is linked over time and stored as individual-level data in subnational or national databases. This system allows for longitudinal tracking of individuals and provides disaggregated data for analysis. Historically, many lowand middle-income countries have relied on aggregate data collected through patient monitoring systems at health facilities. While this approach provides reasonable estimates of progress against key indicators, it does not allow for the collection of individual-level longitudinal data necessary for monitoring program effectiveness. Aggregate data cannot be disaggregated into individual-level data, making it impossible to detect duplicate records, which may lead to overestimation of the number of people diagnosed with HIV and accessing services. Case surveillance addresses some of these limitations by collecting individual-level data, enabling de-duplication of records and linking information across services and facilities using unique identifiers or other person-specific variables. WHO emphasizes the importance of investing in data systems and ensuring interoperability between electronic databases. Open-source standards for data systems are recommended, and WHO suggests allocating 5–10% of program budgets to strengthen monitoring and evaluation efforts. Ethical principles are central to HIV case surveillance. Surveillance activities must prioritize the common good, ensuring that the benefits outweigh individual risks. Equity should be promoted by identifying and addressing health disparities. Respect for persons is essential, involving individuals in decisions that affect them whenever possible. Good governance mechanisms must ensure accountability, transparency, and community engagement. Surveillance policies and procedures should be clearly communicated, and results should be publicly reported in anonymous or aggregate form to empower communities and promote trust. HIV case surveillance systems should collect data on all sentinel events, including HIV diagnosis, entry into care, first CD4 test, ART initiation, viral load tests, and death. For pediatric cases, additional reports are needed for events such as pregnancy, live births to HIV-infected women, and infant PCR test results. Linking maternal and infant data is essential for tracking perinatal transmission and monitoring the impact of prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) programs. Surveillance programs should collect all CD4 and viral load test results to monitor immune function, viral suppression, and continuity of care. Laboratory tests can serve as proxies for care engagement. At a minimum, the CD4 count at entry into care and ART initiation, as well as the date of achieving viral suppression, should be reported. Pediatric HIV surveillance is crucial for determining the burden of infection in children, monitoring maternal transmission, and evaluating PMTCT program effectiveness. HIV case surveillance requires an ethical, legal, and policy framework, standardized case definitions, reporting procedures, data management systems, and robust security measures to protect confidentiality. Surveillance programs must adhere to the highest standards to minimize risks and ensure the confidentiality of reported data. Data analysis should use individual-level data, but only aggregate results and summary statistics should be disseminated to prevent identification of individuals. Surveillance results should be shared with all stakeholders and the public to promote transparency and accountability. Countries should review and update laws, regulations, and policies governing disease reporting to include HIV-related sentinel events. These measures must protect individuals' privacy, ensure data security, and specify how and when surveillance data may be shared or released. All relevant laws, policies, and surveillance methods should be outlined in technical guidance documents accessible to surveillance personnel and the public. HIV case surveillance systems combine demographic, clinical, immunological, and virological information, as well as data on the suspected mode of HIV acquisition. Sentinel events, such as HIV diagnosis, entry into care, first CD4 test, ART initiation, viral suppression, and death, are reported to public health agencies. For pediatric cases, additional events, such as pregnancy and infant PCR test results, are tracked. Surveillance data creates a longitudinal database that follows individuals along the continuum of care, enabling the generation of care cascades and improving program monitoring and evaluation.
